messages.subject: standardized local dependence chi-square according to chen-thissen
parts:
Hi all,

I am using IRTPRO to find the standardized  local dependence chi-square table between my test items. My data is dichotomous(0,1). I am comparing the results IRTPRO produce with my manually obtained results and for some reason I am not getting the same results.

I applied the following steps

1) I started by testing the local dependence chi square test between specific pair of items ( for example item 1 and item 4). I calculated the observed score by calculating the number of students who answered item 1 and item 4 wrong (0,0), item 1 wrong and item 4 right (0,1), item 1 right and item 4 wrong(1,0), item 1 and item 4 are right (1,1).

2) I divided each observed frequency by number of students (88 in my case)

3) to find the expected value for each case (0,0)(0,1)(1,0)(1,1) I calculated the integral chen and thissen produced in their paper between -3 and 3 ability. of course at this stage I have already did model fitting to my data  and I have the item difficulty and item discrimination for item 1 and item 4. 4) then I found the chi square


I hope someone could help me.

I bet IRTPRO is reporting in "standardized" units. That is, you take
your chi^2 stat, subtract the df and divide by sqrt(2*df). That's what
flexMIRT does. I don't understand why they do this instead of converting
to a p-value from the chi^2 distribution directly.

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: standardized local dependence chi-square according to chen-thissen
parts:
The sum of the expectations should equal the sum of the observed values, so if you are working proportions they both should sum to 1. Take a look at mirt's source code to see what is happening internally (and might I suggest using 2x2 tables, conceptually its easier to understand in cases larger than 2x2). https://github.com/philchalmers/mirt/blob/master/R/Exploratory-methods.R

Phil 

P.S. This isn't really a mirt related question or comparison with other software, and probably would be more appropriate on a site like cross-validated.
